title: Contingency Spread Recovery for Public Benefit Pools
one_liner: Zero-upfront PBM pass-through audits sold to school and local-government benefit pools, paid as a share of verified savings, using a shadow pharmacy price list built from local independents' remits, with a slice of each fee paid back to those pharmacies.
customer: Executive directors and boards of multi-employer public benefit pools: school-district benefit trusts and joint powers authorities, county-association and municipal-league health trusts, with 5,000-100,000 lives across dozens of member entities. They buy once for many districts, are subject to open-records and audit pressure, and carry political risk if a PBM overcharge surfaces. Secondary: single counties or districts of 300-3,000 lives (free pilot tier). Payer is the pool, only when savings are verified. No PBM ever pays us.
problem: A pool pays its PBM a billed price per NDC per claim, and its contract may promise pass-through, lowest-of pricing or audit rights. It cannot see what the PBM paid the pharmacy, so the audit rights only test billing against the PBM's own data. Consultants either charge flat fees on PBM-supplied files or are compensated in part by carriers and PBMs (disclosure of broker and consultant compensation is now required under the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act, though disclosure is not independence). Local officials also watch the town's last pharmacy close while the same PBM underpays it. The old obstacle was a claim-level join needing consent from both sides, which is why the parent's tie-out looked hard.
solution: (1) Shadow price list: 20-40 in-region independents contribute NDC-level paid unit price, fill date and BIN/PCN/group only (no patient identifiers), extracted locally. The team reconstructs, by week, what the PBM's retail network actually pays per NDC for the top 200-300 generics that drive most retail generic spend. (2) Tie-out to any plan: take the pool's own claims file (via contractual audit right or public-records request) and compare billed unit price per NDC and date to the reconstructed pharmacy-paid price, producing a spread per member per month by drug. The pharmacies never need to have filled that plan's claims, because a network's pharmacy MAC is common across clients. Scope is stated honestly as retail, and mail and specialty are excluded unless data exists. (3) Screen first: only take pools whose contracts promise pass-through or lowest-of pricing, or who will run an RFP; ordinary legal spread contracts yield renegotiation, not breach recovery. (4) Act: audit-rights letter, renegotiation, or an RFP among 3-5 bidders including the Big 3 and transparent PBMs. (5) Optional Local Access Rider: the pool redirects about 20% of verified savings into a per-Rx access fee paid to in-county independents, a plan-design choice that keeps pharmacies alive and makes them allies. Savings are verified by replaying 12 months post-change against the same shadow list, with a cap.
why_now: Local officials have political will after Rite Aid's exit and Walgreens' closures. Fiduciary and open-records pressure on PBM spend is rising, transparent PBMs give pools credible switch destinations, and federal and state reporting mandates create a paper trail to check (verify current scope). LLM and OCR parsing makes contributing remits a one-day task. January renewals also drive RFP timing, and pools' boards typically decide in Q4-Q1.
revenue_model: Contingency of 12-15% of first-year verified savings, with a floor for pools over 10,000 lives. Illustrative: a 20,000-life pool spends roughly $25-30M a year on drugs; a 4-8% price gap is $1-2M and a 12% share is $120-240k. Recurring Pass-Through Monitor after the audit at about $0.30-0.40 per member per month ($70-95k a year for 20,000 lives). Data co-op dividend: 15-20% of fees paid to contributing pharmacies pro rata as a fair-market-value data license (never tied to referrals; structure with counsel, and keep it away from any federal program business). A few hundred such pools nationally make this a $30M-100M revenue niche.
non_obvious_insight: The employer does not need the claims the pharmacies saw. A PBM's retail pharmacy price list is common across clients in a network tier, so a crowd of pharmacies can reconstruct the hidden list once and any plan's billed prices can be compared to it. That turns a two-party consent-and-join problem into a price-list problem, and each additional pool costs almost nothing to audit. Contingency plus zero PBM money creates the only auditor with clean hands in a field where advisors are paid by the counterparties. Public bodies can compel data that private employers cannot, and the Local Access Rider turns the pharmacies from data suppliers into political allies.
first_30_days: Pick one state with many independents and public pools. Days 1-10: recruit 20 pharmacies through the state association, offering a free margin report in exchange for NDC-level price extracts; build the shadow list for the top 200 generics. Days 10-25: offer one county or district (300-3,000 lives) a free pilot, obtain its claims file by consent or open-records request, and produce a one-page spread letter with a dollars-per-member figure. Days 20-30: take the letter to a pool's executive director and broker and negotiate a contingency letter agreement (12% of verified savings, no fee if zero). Hire a healthcare attorney for data-license and dividend terms. Kill criterion: the pilot shows under 2% spread on retail generics, or fewer than 12 pharmacies agree to contribute.
lineage: mutation of I1266 ('Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch. | How this version avoids them: Truveris and benefits consultants start from what the PBM hands over and charge fixed fees or carry PBM-linked compensation; this starts from the price the pharmacy was actually paid, is paid only on verified savings, and takes no PBM money. They are also possible channel partners for pools that already use them. Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx are the bidders and landing spots the audit sends pools toward, and we take no referral fee from them, which keeps the audit credible; they also cannot verify their own pass-through claims without a third party's pharmacy data. rx-gap-finder is a pharmacy-only underwater-Rx flagger with no employer price side. PQS and CPESN are recruiting channels for pharmacies, not competitors. The target is public pools and counties, a segment the competitor research did not show any of them serving, but this is unverified and should be checked in interviews.

title: Rural County Night Desk for Hospitals and Jails
one_liner: One pool of licensed remote night nurses and NPs sold as a county bundle: the recorded independent second RN for the critical access hospital, and the video screening that lets a deputy clear an arrestee for booking without a four-hour ER trip.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals, county sheriffs and commissioners, state hospital associations, county risk pools, and malpractice and captive insurers, all reached through the same rural-county channels.
problem: At 3am a rural county has three nurses on at the hospital and one or two deputies on the road. The nurse who is supposed to witness a narcotic waste or double-check a high-alert drug is mid-code, and the deputy with an arrestee is stuck in that same ER for hours, leaving the county unpatrolled. Each problem alone is too small to support a dedicated clinical team.
solution: Start with the $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet: a remote RN appears within 60 seconds, watches the waste on video, and attests, with a time-stamped clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet record. Add a booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer) with a physician-signed, ACEP-based clearance protocol and 24/7 RN and NP video screening ('fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', 're-check in 2 hours'). Both run on one recording platform, one compact-licensed clinician pool, one supervising physician and one malpractice policy. The county gets a single dashboard showing diversion-audit coverage, ER visits avoided and 'deputy hours returned to patrol'.
why_now: Rural hospitals are staffed thinly at night and rural jail deaths and diversion are in the news, so both insurers and risk pools are actively looking for evidence-grade controls. Compact licensure and cheap video hardware let a small team run a multi-state night pool for the first time.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month plus per-event fees above volume, and $2,000-3,500 per county per month for about 40 jail screens plus $85 per extra screen, so roughly $4-6k per month for a county bundle. Discounts through malpractice insurers and county risk pools convert to distribution. Gross margin of 40-50% at a pool of about 8-12 hospitals per RN per night.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is the same: a credentialed, recorded, independent clinician on camera at 3am, with a defensible protocol. The evidence infrastructure (timestamped video, audit log, physician-signed protocol) that proves a diversion witness also proves a jail clearance, so one product convinces both insurers. Waste events cluster around medication passes while booking clusters around bar close and weekends, so the two workloads plausibly smooth each other out, and a pilot can confirm that before hiring. The hospital is a natural co-payer, since every cleared arrestee is an ER visit it no longer has to staff for free.
first_30_days: The founder, a rural ER nurse, recruits 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses plus 1-2 NPs on remote night hours. Write the clearance protocol with a supervising rural-ER physician and have one county attorney review it. Pick one county with both a critical access hospital and a jail the founder knows. Offer the hospital a free 30-day cabinet pilot and the sheriff a $1,500, 60-day booking-desk pilot. Bring the combined numbers (waste attestations logged, ER trips avoided, deputy hours saved) to the state hospital association and the county risk pool.
lineage: hybrid of I0016 + I1025 (Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts + Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks). Why stronger: Each parent has the same expensive fixed costs (clinician recruiting, compact licenses, recording platform, physician oversight, malpractice) and a small revenue per site. Pooling spreads those costs over two products sold to overlapping counties, lets one relationship close a larger $4-6k per month deal, and lets two insurers see one shared evidence trail, which raises ACV and lowers cost per sale versus either service alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way. I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: Store Takeover Truth Sheets for Lenders
one_liner: Buyers and lenders of Japanese convenience-store franchise takeovers pay per deal for an independent contract-aware valuation sheet that shows the store's profit after replacing the owner's own labor, under that store's actual royalty and disposal-share terms, plus the ordering upside a new operator could capture.
customer: The payer is the acquirer and its lender, not the incumbent owner. First targets are Kansai multi-store franchise corporations buying additional stores, first-time entrants and second-career buyers taking over a store, and the loan officers at regional banks, shinkin banks and Japan Finance Corporation branches financing them, reached through the founder's own lender and succession advisors. The seller supplies the documents because the sale depends on it.
problem: A store is priced off the HQ-issued statement of 'owner income', which blends profit with wages for unpaid owner and family labor (often 80 to 100 hours a week each) and hides how contract terms bite. At Osaka's 1,231 yen minimum wage, a couple working 140 combined hours a week is worth roughly 9M yen a year before any night premium or manager overhead, so a store showing 10M yen of owner income may earn about 1M yen for a buyer who must hire. A legacy 15/85 disposal contract also hands the buyer 85% of waste risk, while the seller's waste partly reflects HQ-pushed ordering the buyer can change. With Seven's 2027 new contract (50/50, lower charge) never converting existing stores, buyers must now choose between a legacy store and opening a new one on better terms. HQ approves transferees and earns royalties from whoever operates, so it is not a neutral source. Nobody independent computes either adjustment, and this removes the retaliation fear that makes existing owners hard customers.
solution: An 8-page Store Truth Sheet produced in about 5 business days from seller documents (12 months of HQ monthly statements, disposal totals, hourly sales, labor rosters, the franchise agreement). It shows (1) reported owner income restated as profit after paying market-wage replacement labor at current and scheduled minimum wages, (2) royalty tier and disposal-share mechanics for that specific contract, with sensitivity to wage and sales changes, (3) a range for ordering and markdown upside under the new owner's own payoff (the owner-side newsvendor model), (4) remaining term, transfer and renewal-risk flags, and (5) a legacy versus new-store comparison for buyers who could open a fresh store instead. Lenders get a white-label credit-memo version and a 12-month covenant-monitoring option. Later, buyers who close the deal are the natural first customers for the ordering product.
why_now: Three shocks landed together: the 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka, Diamond's report of a Seven internal simulation showing franchisee profit falling to about a third under wage increases, and Seven's June 2026 announcement of a 50/50 contract from autumn 2027 for new stores only. That last one splits the market into legacy and new-contract stores and makes the price of a legacy store genuinely uncertain. Extracting numbers from photographed Japanese statements is now cheap, cutting a manual diligence review that would otherwise be a multi-week accountant job. The store-takeover market is assumed to be growing with owner aging, which needs to be verified before scaling.
revenue_model: 180,000 yen per store diligence sheet paid by the buyer (120,000 yen each when a buyer takes 3 or more stores). Banks that make the sheet a loan condition pay 40,000 yen per file or a per-branch annual license, and can pass it to the borrower. Covenant monitoring at 3,000 yen per store per month for lenders holding loans. Succession advisors who refer deals earn a 10% referral fee. At 10 deals a month this is about 1.8M yen a month, and every sheet adds a contract-parameterized store record to a proprietary benchmark.
non_obvious_insight: The same document set produces two adjustments that point in opposite directions and are both invisible to buyer and seller: owner income falls once labor is priced, and waste upside rises once a new owner uses his own payoff instead of HQ's. Both sides currently negotiate on the HQ statement, so the party with the correct pair of numbers can price a deal better than either side, and a lender will pay for that. Because the buyer pays and has no HQ contract yet, the product sidesteps the fear of OFC retaliation and the franchise-agreement third-party data question is limited to seller-provided records in a sale process. The by-product is a growing cross-store dataset of real royalty, waste and labor economics that nobody outside HQ holds.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: produce Truth Sheets for the founder's own three stores and note the gap between reported income and after-replacement-labor profit. Days 3-10: ask the founder's own lender for a warm introduction to 5 loan officers and reach 3 to 5 succession advisors and multi-store corporations. Publish a free 'profit after replacing yourself' calculator with 6 inputs as the lead magnet. Days 10-30: run 2 free sheets on live deals in exchange for a case study and lender feedback, then sell 3 paid sheets at 180,000 yen (540,000 yen) with a money-back guarantee if the buyer does not find it useful. Kill signal: no live takeover deals found among 15 conversations, in which case the segment volume assumption is false. Also verify seller and HQ data-sharing terms with a franchise lawyer.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified. | How this version avoids them: HQ AI ordering and markdown tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) are operational features with no role in a transaction, and HQ has a conflict as approver and royalty earner. Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine sell operations software to retailers and none values a franchise store. Too Good To Go is a surplus outlet. The union and ex-OFC consultants coach owners on markdowns with no calculators and do not sit on the buy side. Sell-side succession and M&A brokers were not covered in the competitor research and need a check, but by design they are paid on completion by the seller. The only independent buy-side underwriting of contract-adjusted owner economics appears unserved.

title: Cure Desk: Cash-Worker Packets for Health Centers
one_liner: A Spanish-first text-message case tool for health-center enrollment staff that turns a Medicaid noncompliance notice (or a pre-emptive look-back audit) into a state-formatted evidence packet for cash-paid workers, built on batch attestations from the crew leaders, landlords and households who pay them, billed per accepted packet.
customer: Enrollment and patient-navigation managers (certified application counselors, community health worker leads) at FQHCs and community health centers whose panels are heavy with day laborers, house cleaners, landscapers, roofers, temp-agency and informal restaurant workers, and street vendors. Narrow wedge: one Nebraska health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel (plus one refugee language), then a second state that verifies early. The end user is the patient in a 15-minute session with a CHW. The patient installs nothing and pays nothing.
problem: The parent idea was a self-serve wallet sold to MCOs. Judges flagged slow MCO procurement, weak enrollee adoption, and the IFR limiting plans to a support role. The competitor check found SteadyIQ and Emmy giving states free or bundled bank, payroll and gig linking, and Pointcare and Findhelp already holding the FQHC and MCO relationships. What none of them can serve is the worker with no digital trail. The IFR counts self-employment, gig work and in-kind work and lets people combine activities, so someone who cleans three homes for cash and helps on a landscaping crew is legally compliant but has no payroll record, no bank deposits to link, and a 30-day cure clock the day a notice arrives. Timing nuance: an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 (and once per beneficiary in 2028), so the documentation wall arrives in waves. Early-verifying states and audit-driven renewals come first, the general wall later. The first-year job is therefore both cure packets and building an audit-proof evidence file in advance.
solution: Six pieces. (1) Notice intake: the CHW photographs the notice, or the patient forwards it on WhatsApp or SMS. OCR extracts state, case ID, look-back months and deadline, and a 30-day countdown lands in the CHW queue. (2) State evidence rule pack: a maintained library of what each state and program accepts (in-kind work, combined activities, third-party statements, receipts), calibrated by logging every accept and reject reason. (3) Attester rail: the patient names who paid them, and that person gets a text in their own language ('Did Ana Ruiz work for you in August? About how many hours or how much did you pay? Tap to confirm'), creating a timestamped third-party statement in the state's format. Crew leaders, labor contractors, property managers, day-labor centers and church job boards get a batch screen that confirms 5 to 30 workers in one pass, with a reusable profile. (4) Packet: a PDF or portal-ready bundle with the hours or $580 computation, attachments and the patient's e-signature. The CHW submits as authorized representative, and the tool never decides compliance. (5) Outcome capture: accepted or rejected plus the caseworker's reason feeds the rule pack and billing. (6) Routing: patients who do have a digital trail are handed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ consent flow, and exemption flags such as medical frailty are asked as a triage question only.
why_now: The June 3, 2026 IFR sets a Jan 1, 2027 start and a 30-day cure window, and six-month renewals for expansion adults begin around the same time (verify exact start), so notices and renewal checks multiply from Q1 2027. Nebraska is already live and is expected to move from self-attestation to verification. WhatsApp Business API, cheap OCR and LLM translation make a bilingual, photo-based intake cost cents per case, where a bilingual caseworker hour costs roughly $30. That is what makes a 15-minute assisted cure economical for a health center. In 2019 this would have needed a call center.
revenue_model: Per-case fee to the health center: $40 when a packet is opened plus $110 when the state accepts it (max $150, inside the parent's $50-150 range), with a $750 per month per-site minimum. Flat per-case fees rather than percent of Medicaid revenue keep it clean under inducement and billing-agent concerns (healthcare counsel to confirm). Channel revenue: white-label the packet builder as an API or module inside Pointcare, Findhelp or other health-center platforms at a 20-30% revenue share. Illustrative year-1 math (assumptions): 20 health centers x 40 packets a month x $120 average x 12 = about $1.15M. Later: a state-accepted-evidence data license to navigators and legal aid.
non_obvious_insight: Informal work is clustered behind intermediaries. One crew leader, property manager or household employer can attest for many workers at once, so each new attester makes the next patient's evidence nearly free, and the same attester serves patients at other health centers. The hardest segment for bank-linking vendors, where every cash worker is a costly manual exception, becomes the one segment with a network effect. The scarce asset is not the ledger but knowing what each state's caseworkers actually accept, which can only be learned by filing packets and logging outcomes. That data compounds with every case and cannot be bought or scraped.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign one Nebraska FQHC (or health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel) for a free concierge pilot, and call the state Medicaid policy office and two caseworker offices to ask which third-party statements are accepted as evidence. Weeks 2-3: build the flow from a Twilio or WhatsApp number, a Google Form, and a PDF template, with a bilingual attester text. Have the CHW enroll 25 real cash-paid patients and collect at least 40 attestations. Week 4: file the packets, or run the pre-audit in a state that is not yet verifying, and record acceptance rate and CHW minutes per case. Target: 60%+ acceptance and under 30 minutes a case versus 2+ hours today. Then take the numbers to a second health center and to Pointcare and Findhelp as a module partner.
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding. | How this version avoids them: SteadyIQ and CMS Emmy: they win wherever a bank, payroll or gig account can be linked, so Cure Desk does not compete there and routes those patients to their consent flows. It serves only the cash and informal residue, where their cost per case is highest. Free state-side tools and the vendor pledges (Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam) are sold to states and track hours. Cure Desk is a staff workflow sold to health centers. Pointcare and Findhelp: they do lapse detection and dashboards without informal-income packet building, so they are channel partners, not rivals. Propel and mPulse do notices and outreach, and CareRoute is informational. None builds attester-backed evidence. Digital Public Works is a nonprofit focused on mobile income verification. It is adjacent, and could become a partner or a free-riding substitute in some states (risk to monitor). Buyer choice removes the parent's MCO procurement and IFR-role problems.

title: Plug-or-Pitch: Turning Idle Wells Into Assets
one_liner: Screen idle and orphan oil wells for hydrogen, helium and heat evidence, and get paid a share of the plugging liability that disappears when a well is transferred to an explorer who wants a ready-made hole to the basement.
customer: The payer is the liability holder, not the explorer. Wedge: independent operators in Kansas and Oklahoma holding 50-500 idle, shut-in or temporarily abandoned wells under rising plugging and bonding pressure. Phase 2: state orphan-well programs (funded by the $4.7B IIJA orphan-well money) and state land offices. The other side of the transaction, who takes the well and pays a placement fee, is a hydrogen, helium or geothermal junior that today drills new holes at seven-figure cost.
problem: An idle well is a negative asset: plugging often costs tens of thousands of dollars per well (an estimate to confirm state by state), and operators or states carry that liability for years. Meanwhile the parent idea's buyers spend roughly seven figures to drill a test hole to basement, and a wellbore that already penetrates basement, with a file that shows non-flammable gas or elevated temperature, is worth many multiples of its plugging cost to them. The two sides never find each other because the evidence sits in scanned well files, and juniors in the parent's research 'do not budget $15-50k a year for data' but do budget hard money for holes. Price anchored to a known plugging cost is a much easier sale than price anchored to speculative exploration value.
solution: A per-well 'Reuse Dossier' built from each idle well's own file and its offsets: hydrogen/helium/N2-rich gas shows from mud logs, DSTs and driller notes, depth to basement, casing/cement/plugging status, bottom-hole temperature and gradient, and produced-water chemistry, each with page-image provenance and a confidence grade. A Reuse Score estimates re-entry cost against new-drill cost and states the single test that would confirm the lead. Wells are bundled into small re-entry lots and placed with repurposers under a recorded assignment of plugging liability (with state transfer approval and financial assurance), often keeping a retained royalty or carry for the seller. The operator pays nothing upfront: screening is free and the startup is paid from the avoided liability and from the placement. Geothermal scoring can be sourced from partners such as WellScout AI rather than built.
why_now: State and federal pressure on idle wells is at its peak: IIJA orphan-well plugging money is flowing through the late 2020s, and states have built lists that did not exist five years ago. Hydrogen and helium juniors raised $20M-$245M rounds (Koloma, Terra AI, Mantle8) and HyTerra proved that twinning historic wells works, so demand for cheap access to basement-penetrating holes is real. VLM extraction cost per well file has collapsed to a few dollars, which makes free screening for an operator affordable on a contingency basis; that would have been uneconomic in 2022.
revenue_model: Contingent success fee of about 15% of the avoided plugging cost (from the operator or state) when a well transfers, plus a $10-25k placement fee (or 5% of any bonus or sale price) from the repurposer, plus $500-1,500 for a premium dossier and a $10-25k/year 'reuse lot' feed for juniors. Illustrative unit economics: an operator with 200 idle wells costs about $16k to screen (about $80/well compute plus geologist review); if 1-2% clear the bar (1-2 wells above the 0.5% Paris Basin rate is plausible for a targeted fairway) and each saves about $40k of plugging cost, revenue is $6-12k in liability fees plus placement fees per portfolio, and a state program is 10-50x that. The wedge is deliberately contingent so the customer has no downside.
non_obvious_insight: The bid-ask spread has the wrong sign: the holder sees a negative asset (minus the plugging cost) and the explorer sees a hole worth a multiple of its plugging cost, and the only missing ingredient is verified evidence about which wells sit on the positive side. Low hit rate (about 0.5% in the Paris Basin study) kills a subscription atlas but not a contingency screen, because the operator's cost is zero and one hit pays for the portfolio. The startup's true asset is not the data but the transferable, state-approved playbook for liability assignment plus a book of buyers, which creates a two-sided market that data vendors and free datasets cannot replicate.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the public inactive/TA well lists from the Kansas KCC and Oklahoma OCC and pick 300 wells that reach basement in the Nemaha corridor. Week 2: extract their files and offsets and produce 30 Reuse Dossiers with a scored top 10. Week 3: call 25 independent operators and the plugging-fund manager at one state agency with the offer 'give us your 100 worst idle wells, screening is free, we take 15% of the avoided plugging cost if we place a well'. In parallel get 2-3 juniors to sign non-binding LOIs to consider re-entry lots. Week 4: sign 3 contingency agreements and confirm with the state regulator what transfer-with-assumption of liability requires. Before building further, run 15 calls to check the two unverified assumptions: state transfer rules and re-entry cost versus a new drill.
lineage: mutation of I1085 ('Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side. | How this version avoids them: USGS/BLM, KGS, SMU/GDR and GeoMap: free datasets give regional or aggregate layers, none identifies which specific idle well is a transferable reuse candidate, so they are our inputs, not substitutes. WellScout AI is the closest overlap (screens oil wells for geothermal conversion); it covers only heat and sells software to operators, so we can partner on thermal scoring and win on multi-commodity gas evidence plus the transaction. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar keep their data in-house and are demand-side buyers of re-entry lots, not rivals. NthDS and Enverus/TGS sell files to buyers of O&G data; they do not take contingent fees on liability transfers and have channel conflict doing so. AKAP, Wood Mackenzie and Rystad sell market intelligence, not well-level transactions. Not covered in the parent's research and to be verified: oil-and-gas A&D brokers and state orphan-well reuse pilots.

title: Chargeback Network for Aircraft Component Warranties
one_liner: A neutral claims network that moves a failed-repair claim up the chain from operator to pool to shop to piece-part supplier, inside each link's warranty window, with standard reason codes, response clocks and netted settlement. It starts as a back-to-back claim desk for rotable pools.
customer: The first customers are independent rotable pools and Part 145 stations that sell exchange units with warranty downstream and buy repairs with warranty upstream. They are the only parties who are both claimant and respondent. Shops and piece-part suppliers join as respondents, at no cost at first. Operators and lessors join as claimants. Airline procurement teams, lessors and insurers later buy shop-performance data.
problem: One rotable failure triggers a chain of warranties: operator to pool or lessor, pool to shop, shop to piece-part supplier. Each link has its own window, evidence rules, template and email address. The clocks are mismatched. A pool may give the operator a longer window than the shop gives the pool (a typical gap I have not verified). A claim arriving late in the downstream window is already dead upstream, and the pool absorbs the gap. Claims are rejected on paperwork, sent back and forth by email, and never passed up the chain in time. Nobody sees the whole chain. Every party recovers, or fails to recover, alone.
solution: Version 1 is a back-to-back desk for pools. It has an intake address and portal for customer claims. An LLM and rules engine check serial history, the warranty terms and the evidence. Valid claims are auto-converted into a standard upstream packet and sent to the pool's shop inside that shop's window. Invalid claims get a reason-coded response. The desk tracks each claim to a credit and sends a monthly netting statement of credits and debits with each counterparty, settling only the net. Shops receive a complete, pre-checked packet with one-click accept, deny or counter, response timers and a bounded dispute path. In parallel we publish open Rotable Claim Rules v1: reason codes (repeat failure, NFF in warranty, core, turn-time, piece-part defect), an evidence checklist, response clocks such as 10 days to acknowledge and 30 to decide, and a neutral technical panel for disputes. Later layers are shop scorecards for procurement, and advances on approved claims, an early cash payment against approved claims from a small credit facility.
why_now: Cheap LLM reading of repair paperwork, terms and evidence packs makes standard packets and pre-checks possible at low cost per claim. Higher unit values and longer repair turn times since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified) make each missed claim costlier and make pools hold more capital in exchange units.
revenue_model: Pools pay about $45 per claim processed plus 3% of upstream recoveries. Shops with more than 20 claims a month can pay $500-1,500/month for an adjudication assistant. Disputes cost about $250 per panel case. Year 2-3 adds shop-performance data subscriptions: repeat rate by P/N, days to credit, acceptance rate. Later, advances on approved claims at a small monthly discount, a balance-sheet layer priced from our own claim-outcome data.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty chain is a chain of mismatched clocks and formats, and the intermediary pays for the gap. That intermediary is also the one participant who is both claimant and respondent, which is why a pool is the natural seed for a two-sided network, as issuers and acquirers are in card chargebacks. Standard reason codes and evidence rules make a claim cheaper to settle than to fight. Shops gain a filter for invalid claims. At scale the network holds the only serial-level record of repair durability across owners: lemon units, repeat-failure shops and days to credit. No single-company ERP can see that. Defensibility comes from network economies, switching costs in claim histories and netting, and the data.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 pools as design partners, using the free scan from the pool wedge as the way in. Point their customer-claim email address at a shared inbox we monitor. Process claims manually with LLM assistance for 30 days, and send upstream claims in the standard packet to 5 shops. Measure acceptance and days-to-credit against the pool's own baseline. Draft Rotable Claim Rules v0.1 with two retired shop warranty managers as advisors and circulate it to trade groups. Set the target as one upstream credit on a claim that would otherwise have missed its window. Then convert to paid pilots at $2-4k/month across 3-5 pools by month 6.

title: The Pharmacy-Verified Reimbursement Index
one_liner: A furnisher-funded bureau, like a credit bureau for PBM payments, that turns what pharmacies actually pay and are actually paid into a reference index that state laws, Medicaid rate-setting and transparent-PBM contracts can cite, launching with a per-state Underwater Index sold to pharmacy associations for the 2027 legislative sessions.
customer: First six months: state pharmacy associations and their legal and lobbying arms in 3-5 states with active 2027 PBM agendas, at $25-60k per state per year. Next: state Medicaid pharmacy programs and state employee plans rebasing dispensing fees and ingredient-cost basis, departments of insurance enforcing below-cost and pay-parity laws, and TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs that want an external yardstick. Eventually: contracts that reference the index directly. Contributing pharmacies pay nothing and get a dividend.
problem: Everyone who needs a reference price for pharmacy reimbursement relies on an interested party or a slow survey. NADAC is a voluntary survey of acquisition costs that says nothing about dispensing cost or what any PBM actually paid. State cost-of-dispensing studies are periodic, commissioned from consultants, and stale by publication (typically low-to-mid six figures each; verify). Legislators cannot say how many claims are paid below cost or by whom, so reimbursement-floor and pay-parity laws are enforced only by complaint. PBMs face no neutral definition of a fair payment. The parent's insight (pharmacies hold the ground-truth ledger) is stronger as infrastructure than as a one-off audit.
solution: Pharmacies use the free local-first margin report (same ingestion as a per-pharmacy tool) and opt in to contribute monthly aggregates: paid price and invoice cost per NDC per PBM network per state, plus optionally allocated cost-to-dispense. The bureau publishes: (a) a State Underwater Index (share of claims paid below acquisition cost, by PBM, only where 10+ pharmacies and 5+ per PBM cell contribute, with a 90-day lag); (b) an invoice-based acquisition cost index by NDC-week; (c) a quarterly cost-of-dispensing panel; (d) a regulator API to test whether a network paid below the index in a given month. Design floor for antitrust: a third-party-run exchange following the withdrawn 1996 health-care information-exchange conditions (5+ contributors, no contributor over 25% weight, data 3+ months old), plus counsel sign-off. Credibility: published methodology, an independent standards board (pharmacist, health economist, antitrust counsel, ex-regulator) and a sample audit by an accounting firm. Flywheel: an association buys the evidence pack, a law cites the index, the regulator needs the feed, contracts reference the index, and more pharmacies contribute for the dividend (25% of index revenue, pro rata by verified contribution).
why_now: A wave of state PBM reimbursement and transparency laws has arrived just as closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores, Drug Channels' August 2026 'K-shaped shakeout') give legislators a reason to demand numbers; 2027 sessions open in January and associations need evidence in Q4. The cost stack has collapsed: surveying a few hundred pharmacies by questionnaire costs six figures, but reading remits and invoices they already hold costs cents per claim now that OCR and LLM parsing handle messy formats and local-first processing removes the custody objection. This is a 2026 unlock, not a 2019 one.
revenue_model: Association evidence pack plus monthly index: $25-60k per state per year (target 3 states by month 6, about $100-150k). State Medicaid and employee-plan data licenses: $100-400k per state per year after a track record. DOI compliance feed: $50-150k. API licenses for TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs: $25-100k. Index-in-contract licensing: about $0.02-0.05 per member per month, comparable to index-licensing models in other markets. Pharmacies: free plus a 25% revenue dividend. A 30-state footprint could plausibly support $10-30M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Standards win by being cited in statutes and contracts, and NADAC became the reference by being neutral, not by being complete. A pharmacy-verified index earns legitimacy differently, because it comes from invoices and remits (facts, not survey opinion), and it is the only source that can measure paid versus cost per PBM, which is exactly what a below-cost reimbursement law needs in order to be enforced. Associations fund the first index as lobbying evidence, the resulting laws then create a compliance buyer (the regulator), and each citation adds switching cost. The more PBM-owned pharmacies dominate the market, the more the independents' ledger is the only independent counterfactual.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 2 states with an active 2027 PBM agenda and pitch the association executive directors: 'your state's Underwater Report by December 15 for session prep, co-branded.' Days 5-25: recruit 25 contributing pharmacies per state with a free margin report; run 6 months of remits and invoices through a local script by hand (concierge). Days 10-20: retain antitrust counsel for a 10-page methodology and thresholds memo, and seat a 5-person advisory board. Day 20-30: ask a state DOI or Medicaid pharmacy director for a 30-minute meeting on what they would need to enforce existing rules. By day 30: 2 signed letters of intent at about $25k and 40 contributing pharmacies. By day 60: first anonymized state index published. Kill criterion: no association will pay $25k for a state report before the session opens.

competition_context:

title: 48-Hour Verify List for Independent Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: A daily, capacity-capped list of the specific floored VINs an independent lender's auditor should physically verify in the next 48 hours, built from listing disappearance plus the lender's own payoff ledger, with a disposition classifier and per-dealer baselines that fix the noisy-signal problem.
customer: Head of collateral or audit (CRO as signer) at independent used-car floorplan lenders with roughly $30M to $500M outstanding across 100 to 1,500 independent and buy-here-pay-here dealers, plus credit unions and community banks with dealer floorplan lines. It deliberately excludes franchised new-car dealers, where captives already get retail delivery reports and can build this in-house. Secondary channel is regional floorplan audit firms that dispatch for-cause audits.
problem: An independent lender has a handful of auditors and hundreds of dealers, so the Monday question is not 'is there fraud' but 'which 12 VINs at which 4 dealers do I visit this week'. The judges' flaws map onto this. (1) A raw 'VIN left the website' flag is noisy, since the car may be wholesaled, transferred to a sister lot, in recon or never listed. (2) A fixed 7 to 10 day payoff window misfires on slow-funding but honest dealers. (3) A standalone radar dashboard is one more screen for a team with no data scientists. (4) The $15 to $30 per dealer price is unvalidated. (5) It misses double-flooring, which was most of Sky Auto Mall.
solution: Data need is one file: the lender's daily list of active floored VINs (VIN, dealer, floor date, advance), exported as a flat file from any core system. A VIN dropping off that file means it was paid, so no payoff-event integration is needed. Listing history comes from a licensed feed (a MarketCheck-type source scanning 100k+ dealer sites daily), plus a crawl of only the lender's own dealers' public sites, which the lender's dealer agreement can require them to permit. (a) A disposition classifier sorts every vanished floored VIN into transfer to a sister store, appears at auction or wholesale, relisted, or 'retail-sale signature' (gone, no reappearance, often after a pending or price-change state). Only the last type with an open balance enters the queue. (b) Each dealer gets its own baseline lag distribution of delist-to-payoff days learned over 90 days, and the flag fires on deviation from that dealer's own pattern, not a fixed window. (c) The output is capped to the lender's audit capacity, for example 'you have 3 auditor-days: here are the 12 VINs at 4 dealers with the highest expected loss', with a timestamped listing-history evidence pack and a one-click verify request that can go to the lender's own auditors or an audit vendor. (d) An optional second signal is title or lien-release data where lawfully obtainable, but v1 does not depend on it.
why_now: Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025) and the Sky Auto Mall litigation (Ford Credit and Stellantis, March 2026) made every lender's risk committee ask what they know between audits. Inventory sits near 88 days' supply with floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps, so dealers lean harder on lines. Licensed daily dealer-site listing history now exists off the shelf, and LLM extraction makes normalizing messy dealer pages cheap for a team of three. Vero's April 2026 content says bank dealer-services teams want to 'automate audit triage and SOT reporting', which confirms the buyer's framing.
revenue_model: Platform fee of about $1,500 to $3,000 per month per lender, sized to dealer count and booked against the audit budget, plus a catch fee of about $250 per VIN later confirmed unpaid-sold by the lender's own ledger and caught before its next scheduled audit. A backtest-based 'retro-scan' is priced at $5k and credited against year one. A lender with 300 dealers pays roughly $40k to $60k per year. A first-two-years target of 40 to 60 lenders and credit unions implies roughly $2M to $3.5M ARR. These are assumptions to validate, not findings.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's payoff ledger is free data hiding in plain sight: a VIN leaving the daily floored-VIN file is the payoff event, so the product needs one CSV, not a core-system integration. The real product is dispatch, not detection. Auditors only pay for a signal that changes whom they visit this week, and the noise is tamed by comparing each dealer to its own delist-to-payoff habits rather than to a global threshold, and by refusing to alert unless the disposition looks like a retail sale.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2, backtest on public cases (Sky Auto Mall filings and a few others) using historical listing data to show fire dates versus discovery dates. In parallel, interview five lender audit or risk heads to confirm the ranked list would change their audit order. Weeks 2 to 4, sign three small independent floorplan lenders or credit unions to a free retro-scan. They send 12 months of daily floored-VIN files plus their known SOT events. Report recall, false alerts per 100 dealers per week and median days of lead time over their actual discovery. Offer a free 60-day live shadow run, converting to platform plus catch fee only after at least one real catch. Also ask two audit firms for a for-cause dispatch partnership.
lineage: mutation of I0218 ('Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount.
