Double-flooring stays out of scope here (it is the seed of a later cross-lender feature), so precision claims stay honest.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Highland Electric Fleets, Hyroad Energy, Phoenix Motor (Phoenix Motorcars) / Proterra transit, Lion Bus (post-bankruptcy Lion Electric). White space: Not found in this research: any player selling a brand-agnostic, per-bus sustainment contract with an availability guarantee and a pooled spares inventory for orphaned electric school buses. Highland offers a guarantee for buses it deploys and Hyroad does the estate-buying for hydrogen trucks, but neither was found serving orphaned Lion buses. Herscher CUSD (IL), Winthrop (MA) and Yarmouth (ME) are paying ad hoc 'alternate vendors' or have parked buses, and the Electrek piece names no third-party service provider. The wedge is Lion's US-orphaned school buses. That is a small installed base, described only as 'dozens of districts', and its sizing was not verified. Multi-district pooling through a state agency or regional service center is also unserved. Caveats: this verdict comes from a thin evidence base, because the WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) and only about a dozen direct page fetches worked. No search of Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or open-source tools was possible. Small independent EV repair shops, dealers or school-bus contractors may already do this informally and would not show up in homepage fetches. Weaknesses in the idea: (a) the 'buy the estate cheaply now' premise looks partly stale, since Lion's US facilities were divested by mid-2025 and its Chapter 15 dates to Dec 2024, so the parts and tooling may already be sold; (b) Proterra transit has a successor OEM in Phoenix Motor; (c) battery, BMS and inverter repair on reverse-engineered buses carries fire and liability risk, given the EPA investigation of Lion bus fires and Quebec pulling Lion buses out of service; (d) the buyer pool is small and public budgets are slow.

title: Private Road Agreements That Save Rural Closings
one_liner: A flat-fee e-sign-and-record service that produces the road-maintenance and shared-well agreements lenders demand, then turns each road into a dues-collecting association.
customer: Listing and buyer agents and title/escrow officers in rural and mountain markets (CO, MT, ID, WA, OR, UT, NC/TN mountains, northern New England) pay $400-750 per transaction. Later, the households on each road pay $15-40 a month through the association.
problem: A house on a private road often has no enforceable maintenance agreement, only a handshake among neighbors. FHA, VA, USDA and most conventional underwriters want a recorded, legally enforceable agreement, and similar paper for shared wells, septics and driveways. The appraiser flags the private road and the problem lands on nobody. It surfaces 7-10 days before closing, the neighbors have no reason to cooperate, and the deal slips or dies. Between sales the road decays because nobody can collect dues.
solution: Software plus templated law. (1) Detect private vs public roads from county GIS and identify every benefiting parcel and owner. (2) Use state-specific agreement templates reviewed once by local counsel. (3) Run a multi-party e-sign, remote online notarization and e-recording workflow with a friendly neighbor-outreach script. (4) Add a lender-ready cover letter that answers the standard underwriting condition. (5) Upsell to a formal road association (entity, EIN, bank account, ACH dues billing, reserve tracking, lien rights where state statute allows) and shared well/septic agreements.
why_now: Affordability pushes buyers toward exurban and rural homes, and many of them rely on FHA, VA or USDA financing with strict access rules. Remote online notarization and e-recording are now legal and routine in most states. Counties are refusing to accept new roads into public maintenance. Wildfire-zone insurers and fire districts increasingly care about year-round road access and maintenance.
revenue_model: $495 flat per agreement package, paid by the seller through escrow or by a title partner, plus pass-through recording fees. $250 add-on per shared well, septic or easement agreement. Recurring: $29/month association software plus a payment fee on dues (about 3% + $3 per household per month). Referral fees from title partners.
non_obvious_insight: The road is not the deal-killer. The 4-30 neighbors who each have zero incentive to sign are. So the product is the neighbor-consent workflow, not the document. The other insider fact is that underwriters usually accept a simple recorded agreement signed by a majority of owners with proportional cost shares. You don't need a full HOA. Once a road has bank-account-backed dues, it becomes a sticky recurring customer that nobody else serves.
first_30_days: Pick 2 counties dense with private roads (for example the foothills of Larimer/Boulder CO, or Flathead MT). Pull active listings and cross-match them to county road-class GIS to find listings on private roads. Pay a local real-estate attorney about $2-3k to review one template. Cold-contact those listing agents with a specific message: your listing is on a private road, the lender will ask for this, and we deliver in 7 days. Sign 5 pilots at $495 and 2 title officers as referral partners.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Other small-HOA software (Buildium, AppFolio, HOA Start, Vantaca, Cinc and similar), Local real-estate attorneys and title/escrow companies (the incumbent workaround), Generic legal-form sellers (LegalZoom, US Legal Forms, Rocket Lawyer). White space: Only partly verified: the WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so I could not check for a funded startup, Product Hunt or YC listing, or forum demand. I used direct page fetches and a GitHub search instead. What I found: (1) No direct competitor turned up in direct fetches, and GitHub has no open-source project for this. (2) The per-deal neighbor-consent workflow (identify benefiting parcels from county GIS, outreach script, multi-party RON/e-sign, e-record, lender cover letter) appears unserved by software. Today it is handled by attorneys and title officers by hand, with generic templates from form sellers. (3) The recurring association layer is NOT white space. PayHOA serves 0-25 unit associations at $49/mo with $2.45 flat ACH, against the idea's $29/mo plus 3% + $3 per household (about $3.45-4.20 on a $15-40 dues payment), so the idea's layer costs more per household than the incumbent. (4) The lender-demand premise is weaker than stated. The HUD Handbook 4000.1 text I could read (2019 edition, p.184 and p.566 of the PDF) requires private streets to be protected by a permanent recorded easement, ownership interest, or HOA ownership, says shared driveways do NOT require a joint maintenance agreement, and only has the appraiser ask whether a maintenance agreement exists and comment on road condition. So for FHA the real deal-killer is a missing recorded easement (a title/access cure), not the maintenance agreement. I did not verify VA, USDA or conventional rules or any newer HUD revision. The defensible unserved wedge is a title-partner-distributed neighbor-consent and recording workflow for lenders and loan types that do require the agreement, plus an easement/access cure.

title: The Reference Panel: Neutral Ruler for E/M Levels
one_liner: A neutral, triple-blind coder-and-physician panel that measures how reliable any E/M level really is, and sells that measurement to scribe vendors, payers and providers who are now fighting over it.
customer: Three sides. First payer: health-system and large-group compliance and counsel with contested encounters (payer record requests, downcode appeals, OIG inquiries). Second: scribe and coding-AI vendors that need independent validation. Third: payers running automated downcoding, which face state laws and regulator scrutiny on human review. Auditors and RCM firms become licensees.
problem: E/M level is a judgment, not a fact. Published studies show weak agreement even among trained coders: one study had five experienced certified coders assign codes to six notes and only one code was unanimous, and another found 36% inter-rater reliability among eight research nurses across 4,137 visits. Yet three AI systems now assign levels (scribes, autonomous coders, payer downcoders) and contradict each other. Each treats its own output as truth, and extrapolated overpayment demands multiply one reviewer's noise across a whole claims universe. Nobody publishes the noise floor, so the dispute goes to whoever has more lawyers.
solution: An independent panel of certified coders plus a physician advisor labels encounters blind against the 2021 MDM and time rules, with adjudication and published agreement statistics (Krippendorff's alpha by specialty and level). An AI pre-read and single coder handle easy cases and only disagreements escalate to a three-person panel, so the average is about 1.6 reviews per encounter. Product ladder: (a) 'Panel-Certified Level' files for contested encounters, giving a level, a confidence and dissent notes, at $60-90 each; (b) annual validation of a vendor's or payer's AI against a held-out panel-labeled set with a published scorecard, $75-200k a year; (c) noise-floor benchmark subscription and consortium membership at $25-50k; (d) later, a licensed evaluator model trained on the adjudicated labels. Governance rules that make it credible: published methodology, physician advisory board, no vendor equity, no single side above 30% of revenue.
why_now: In 2025-26 three sets of AI systems are assigning and contesting E/M levels at scale. Payers' automated downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025) is reported, as are state downcoding laws in Arkansas and Virginia, with more pending. Scribe vendors are advertising 'audit-ready' and 'verified' accuracy. The 'coding arms race' is in the literature. Each side needs a ground truth it can cite, and the trailing 12 months are when disputes and vendor procurement turn to evidence.
revenue_model: Contested-encounter certification at $60-90 per encounter is the first revenue, with cost near $15-25 including adjudication, so about 70% gross margin. Vendor and payer validation at $75-200k a year. Benchmark and consortium memberships at $25-50k a year. Later licensing of the evaluator model. Revenue mix goal is roughly a third from each of providers, vendors and payers to keep neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: The product is the disagreement rate. Once you can say 'certified coders disagree on this specialty's level-4 encounters 30% of the time', a single-reviewer downcode or a single-reviewer audit finding falls inside the noise floor, and an extrapolated overpayment should shrink, which is worth real money to providers. It also turns every incumbent into a customer. VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity, Charta and the AI coders can each validate against or license the panel, so none of them needs to see it as an attack. Credibility is the moat and scales with every adjudicated encounter.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 CPC/CPMA coders and one physician advisor. Approach two health-system compliance teams that have open payer record requests or downcode disputes and offer to triple-blind review 100 contested encounters each at a pilot rate ($8-15k). Publish a 6-page methodology paper and the first anonymized agreement statistics. Offer two scribe or coding-AI vendors a 200-encounter validation on the understanding that results are only published with consent. Aim for one paid pilot and one vendor letter of intent.
lineage: mutation of I0389 ('Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface. | How this version avoids them: It does not compete as another audit platform or AI coder. VMG Health, MDaudit and Healthicity run single-reviewer workflows for one side, so they cannot be neutral, and they are natural licensees and second-opinion buyers. Ambience (95% 'AAPC-verified'), Abridge and DeepScribe self-attest, and the panel is the independent replacement for that claim. Fathom, Arintra and CodaMetrix have the same conflict. Trilliant publishes descriptive studies but has no panel-labeled ground truth. BCBSA and payer AI programs are the counterparty and become customers for calibration. Riskiest assumption is that all sides will accept a neutral panel, which is why the first product is the per-encounter certification that pays before neutrality is proven.

title: Pumper-Sampled Hydrogen and Helium Ground-Truth Registry
one_liner: Stop digging through what the industry failed to measure and start measuring it: pay lease pumpers to grab wellhead gas samples, assay them for hydrogen and helium, and build the depth-tagged registry that becomes the standard for what is under the ground.
customer: Wedge: hydrogen, helium and geothermal explorers and their modelers (Koloma-type juniors outside their own acreage, HyTerra/MAX Power-type juniors, Terra AI, HyReveal) who commission sampling campaigns across a fairway. Contributors: small independent operators and the pumpers (lease operators) who visit each well weekly, starting with the Kansas and Oklahoma independents. Later payers: lenders, insurers and resource certifiers who need a standard, auditable measurement before they finance a discovery.
problem: Old well files are noisy for a structural reason: the industry never measured hydrogen or helium. Standard mud-logging and production gas analysis use flame-ionization detectors that cannot see H2 or He, so a 1935 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' note is an accident, contamination and sampling method are unknown, and the parent's archive is capped at about 16,000 free analyses and a 0.5% hit rate. Explorers who need to know where hydrogen and helium are today either drill blind, run private one-off campaigns, or use soil-gas anomalies. Nobody keeps a standardized, depth-tagged, contamination-corrected, fresh measurement for the roughly one million producing US wells or the tens of thousands of new holes drilled each year.
solution: A three-layer business. Layer 1 (first product, sellable in 6 months): buyer-commissioned sampling campaigns. A buyer specifies a transect or 200-well fairway; operators allow their pumpers to fill a $12 sample container at the casinghead or separator vent following a safety protocol; a bounty of about $25 goes to the pumper; samples go to a partner lab or an in-house GC-TCD unit, and the buyer gets H2/He/N2/CO2/Ar/O2/C1-C6 with GPS, photo, chain of custody and an air-contamination correction. Layer 2: a registry with an open measurement spec (sampling method, contamination QC, lab certification) and a contribution scheme: operators get a free full gas assay (which many already pay $50-150 for to support BTU, sales or flaring reports, a hypothesis to test), exclusive rights to their own well results for 90-180 days, and a revenue share. Layer 3: a certified add-on H2/He TCD channel for mud-logging contractors and geothermal drillers so every new hole feeds the registry, and a scoring layer that uses fresh samples to calibrate the archive-based confidence grades from the parent idea.
why_now: Hydrogen and helium explorers are funded (Koloma about $245M, Mantle8 EUR31M, Terra AI $20M with BHP and Khosla, 123 companies per AKAP) but starved of trustworthy labels, and the modelers (Terra AI, HyReveal) explicitly need fresh ground-truth data. Portable micro-GC/TCD analyzers and smartphone chain-of-custody have made distributed sampling cheap, and VLM tools make the old archive a cheap starting prior rather than the product. Geothermal and helium buyers want auditable data for financing, and no standard exists yet, which is the moment a standard can be set.
revenue_model: Sampling campaigns at about $250 per well (cost roughly $60-120 with in-house GC and $130-170 with outside labs); a 200-well campaign is about $50k. Registry subscriptions of $10-50k per basin per year for explorers and modelers. Data licenses to modelers and financiers. Lab certification and channel fees from mud-logging contractors. Optional later: small overriding royalties on leases taken over registry-flagged sections. Year-1 target: 1,500-3,000 wells sampled, 5-8 campaign customers (about $300-400k), 10 registry subscribers.
non_obvious_insight: The right inversion is that data quality, not data availability, is the bottleneck: every archive layer the parent proposed is limited by a measurement nobody made. Because operators pay for gas analysis anyway, the marginal cost of adding H2 and He to a routine sample is almost zero, so the contributor network can be built with a bounty rather than a salesforce. The registry's moat is network economics plus a standard: contributors are also the sources, the modelers need the labels, and lenders will trust the one dataset with certified provenance. Fresh samples also calibrate the archive-derived confidence scores, so the parent idea becomes a cheap prior on top of a proprietary ground-truth set.
first_30_days: Week 1: contract a commercial gas lab that runs GC-TCD (or buy a used micro-GC with TCD for about $15-25k) and design the sample kit and safety protocol with an experienced pumper. Week 2: sign 2 independent operators (about 100 wells each, via the Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association and personal referrals) on the free-assay, 90-day-exclusive deal. Week 3: sample 100 wells across a transect crossing the Nemaha uplift and publish a one-page ground-truth map. Week 4: pitch 15 juniors and modelers a 200-well campaign at $250 per well with half prepaid, and ask HyReveal and Terra AI for a data-partner letter. Kill test: if no buyer prepays by week 6, sell the same samples as a section-level pack to landmen (see the sharpened offspring).
lineage: mutation of I1085 ('Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side. | How this version avoids them: USGS/BLM (about 16,000 historical analyses, 2021) and KGS OFR 2025-59: static, mixed-quality historical compilations; our data is new, standardized and continuously growing, with QC they lack. SMU/GDR and GeoMap: temperature-focused and free; we sell direct gas chemistry. Heologic (helium-anomaly database and consulting): relies on subsoil helium proxies and sells services; we measure at-depth well gas at scale through a contributor network and an open spec. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar: proprietary data only in their own footprints; they become campaign buyers outside their acreage. Terra AI and HyReveal: modelers who lack labels, so they are customers and channel partners rather than competitors. NthDS and Enverus/TGS: software and data resellers with no field measurement network and no reason to build one, likely acquirers. Zanskar and WellScout AI: focused on geothermal; not a gas registry.

title: Retailer-Mandated Vulnerability Desk, Paid by Suppliers
one_liner: EU retailers and distributors put the desk on their approved-provider list for connected private-label and marketplace products, and their non-EU suppliers pay per SKU family, the way suppliers already pay retailer-nominated test labs, while the retailer gets a live exposure dashboard for its whole connected catalogue.
customer: Mandating party: product-compliance heads at mid-size EU consumer-electronics, DIY, sports (e-bikes), toy and discount retailers and distributors with 50-2,000 connected SKUs, including own-brand ranges. Payers: the 20-200 non-EU suppliers and ODMs behind those SKUs, each paying for the product families it sells to that retailer.
problem: A retailer that sells connected products under its own name is treated as the CRA manufacturer (to confirm with counsel), and an importer or distributor must chase unreachable non-EU suppliers when a vulnerability appears. Retailers have no view of which of their 1,800 connected SKUs contain the component in this morning's exploited-vulnerability headline. Their suppliers will not share firmware willingly and cannot show a 24h capability. The parent's problem is that small makers will not buy a desk they see as insurance. Here the party with the pain is not the party with the budget, and the retailer holds the leverage over the supplier.
solution: Product 1 is a retailer-paid 'Connected Range Exposure Baseline'. The desk collects firmware for 25-50 SKUs, which the retailer can compel from suppliers. It unpacks them, builds the component lists, checks current exposure to KEV/EUVD, tests each supplier's vulnerability-contact deliverability, and delivers a supplier-requirement clause for the next supplier manual. Product 2 is the ongoing service. The retailer's supplier manual names the desk (and any equivalent that passes its audit) as an approved provider. Each supplier enrols product families and the desk becomes its AR and 24/7 filing service, with stack-pooled triage. The retailer sees a live dashboard: for each SKU, affected, not affected or unknown, with supplier response time, supporting delist or recall decisions and its own regulatory file. The desk's fan-out model is reused, but the sales motion is one retailer mandate that brings in many suppliers.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live since 11 Sep 2026 and retailer supplier manuals are being rewritten ahead of Dec 2027. RED delegated-act cybersecurity rules (in force since Aug 2025) and GPSR (since Dec 2024) have already taught retail compliance teams to demand supplier documents and chase non-EU suppliers, so the workflow and budget owner exist. Retail groups have not yet named a vulnerability-reporting provider, so early mandates set the approved list.
revenue_model: Retailer-paid baseline of EUR 10-25k per range as the first sale. Dashboard licence of EUR 15-40k/yr per retailer. Supplier-paid subscription of EUR 600-1,200 per product family per year (falling with volume), plus EUR 1.5-3k per filing event, contractually paid by the supplier. One mid-size retailer with about 150 connected SKU families across 60 suppliers yields roughly EUR 100-130k/yr. Ten retailers gives roughly EUR 1M+ ARR with sales cost amortised across 60 or more payers per mandate.
non_obvious_insight: Change the buyer chain, not the product. Retail supply chains already run on the 'nominated lab' pattern, where the buyer mandates a provider and the supplier pays, and testing spend per product (EN 18031 or similar) dwarfs a EUR 600-1,200 annual desk fee, so suppliers barely resist. The dashboard turns a rare-event insurance product into something a compliance head opens every morning. And retail is the only place where a 24/7 filer has real leverage, because the retailer can delist a supplier that does not respond.
first_30_days: Identify 15 EU retail and distribution product-compliance heads via GPSR, RED and product-safety forums and trade-association events. Pitch each a EUR 12k baseline on 25-50 own-brand SKUs, with the deliverable being an exposure table plus supplier scorecard plus draft supplier-manual clause. Publish the clause as a free template through retail associations to seed demand. Sign 2 paying baselines by day 30-45. Use the baselines to build the first supplier cohorts (20-40 suppliers) and open partnership talks with SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas and TUV, who hold the current nominated-lab relationships, about white-labelling the 24/7 back end.
lineage: mutation of I0374 ('Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: None of the competitors in the parent's research sells to retailers. Finite State, Cybellum, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, EcoComply, H-X and the SBOM vendors all sell to manufacturers one at a time, paying a high customer-acquisition cost per maker, and Patchstack is free and open-source only. One retailer mandate replaces dozens of separate maker sales. The obvious threat is certification bodies and labs, which sell one-off per-model reports while a 24/7 desk has the opposite cost structure, so they are better treated as distribution partners. Switching costs come from integration with the retailer's PLM and supplier-onboarding flow, and from the supplier cohort already enrolled, which a copycat would have to win over from scratch.

title: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors
one_liner: A neutral calculation agent runs a county-approved, developer-funded home-value guarantee for houses near proposed data centers, using pre-announcement baselines and public sale records with no sensors, and unspent escrow reverts to the developer, which makes it cheaper than $10k checks and more credible.
customer: Payer: independent data center developers and their CFOs and general counsel, especially those that have already tried lump-sum checks or buyouts and got 'bribe' coverage (NorthPoint-type offers, Mason County-type buyouts). Co-signer: county commissions that put the guarantee into a development agreement. Distribution partners: title and escrow companies, mortgage lenders and local realtors in the impact radius, who deliver claims at the point of sale. Beneficiaries: owner-occupants within roughly 1-3 miles.
problem: Residents' biggest fear is not a sensor reading, it is the value of their house. Developers are already spending on this fear in the worst way: NorthPoint's $10k-per-household offer ($45M across 4,500 households) was called a bribe, and Propmodo expects future offers to move to 'utility bill credits or property value guarantees rather than lump sums'. A check pays 100% of households for a risk that only touches the minority who sell at a loss, buys no trust, and leaves the price question unresolved. Home-value anecdotes are contested (a 4-bedroom listed 15-18% lower next to a Northern Virginia hyperscale site; the NAR 2026 Data Center Impact Report and local reporting disagree on how far effects reach), so both sides are arguing about a number nobody has pre-agreed.
solution: Product: a Property Value Assurance Program administered as a contract, not insurance. The developer is the obligor and funds an escrow (illustratively $3-5k per eligible household, against $10k of certain checks) with a corporate escrow agent at signing of the development agreement. We are the neutral calculation agent, the way a calculation agent works in a structured contract. Mechanics: (1) Freeze a reference value for each enrolled home at the date of first public disclosure of the project, using an AVM plus a broker price opinion (about $300), with a full appraisal only if disputed. (2) Publish a county-wide control index (repeat-sales or hedonic, plus matched control neighborhoods) so market moves are separated from project effects. (3) If the owner sells at arm's length within 10 years (listed 60+ days, arm's-length buyer), we pay from escrow the shortfall between the net sale price and the control-index-adjusted reference value, up to a cap (for example 20% of reference). (4) Unspent escrow reverts to the developer at year 10, or is split with a community fund. (5) No sensors: the trigger is a price versus a pre-agreed formula, so there is no argument about causation, only about arithmetic. Adverse selection and gaming are handled with the arm's-length rule, an exposure cap and a three-appraiser tie-break (already the norm in Mason County buyouts).
why_now: In 2026 lump-sum neighbor payments went mainstream and drew immediate backlash (NorthPoint, September 2026 coverage), while moratoria in NY (July 14) and Texas (Sept 21) plus local pauses give developers a reason to look for a structure that survives a hearing. Data-center adjacency is now a mainstream real-estate question: Realtor.com counts 108 ZIP codes with a large data center by June 2026, up from 12 in 2015, and NAR and HousingWire are publishing on it, so buyers and lenders already ask. AVMs, MLS and deed data are cheap and standardized. Wind developers have used property-value guarantees as permit conditions, so counties and lawyers recognize the form.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer from the program budget. Illustrative 3,000-household program: $300 per household enrollment (AVM, BPO, lien check, portal) = $900k; 1% per year of a $12M escrow = $120k; $1,500 per adjudicated sale claim; optional 50 bps share of escrow yield (T-bill yield on $12M is meaningful float for the agent-of-record bank to share). Roughly $1M+ of year-one revenue per program, about 10x the parent's $75-150k sensor setup, with software-like margins after the model is built. Second revenue line: sell the control-index and price-effect research to counties, lenders and appraisers. Assumptions to test: 10-25% of homes sell within 10 years and only some at a shortfall; expected payout 10-30% of escrow.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is cheaper for the developer than a check and more persuasive to the neighbor, at the same time: the expected payout is only the shortfall on homes that actually sell at a loss, and unspent money returns, while residents receive the thing they said they wanted (protection of value, per Propmodo) instead of hush money. It also sidesteps the attribution trap that hurts the parent, because the trigger is a formula on public deed data, not a causal claim about a well or a hum. And it aligns incentives: every year the facility runs quietly is a year the developer's escrow is not drawn, so neighbors and developer want the same outcome. Making the developer the obligor also removes the insurance-law problem the parent's escrow payout faced.

Days 15-30: pitch two county attorneys with pending hearings; line up a corporate escrow agent and one title company. Target: a letter of intent for a 300-household pilot with a $1M escrow. title: Well Covenant Trustee for Rural Data Center Counties
one_liner: A neutral program administrator writes, monitors and runs a county-mandated, developer-funded private-well protection covenant, where excess drawdown versus upgradient control wells triggers in-kind remediation with no lawsuit and no sensor sales.
customer: Wedge: county attorneys and planning directors in rural, private-well counties that are already drafting developer-funded monitoring and neighbor-escrow language (Franklin County IN draft v3.0, Shenandoah County VA, and similar counties in GA, PA and IN). Payer: the independent developer of a 50-500 MW campus in that county, which funds the covenant because the county makes it a permit or development-agreement condition. Not hyperscalers with in-house community teams.
problem: Dry or silted wells are what actually produce lawsuits and hearing revolts (Meta / Newton County GA: neighbors say wells went dry, Meta's own study says groundwater flows away, families sued in Sept 2026). Nobody can separate data-center drawdown from drought or other pumping, so developer-commissioned studies are not believed and neighbor claims cannot be proven. Counties are drafting escrow and monitoring language from scratch, with no tested trigger, no neutral administrator and no legal structure. The parent's sensor-baseline product is a crowded, commoditizing layer (KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, consultancies), and its automatic cash payout risks being classed as insurance or read as an admission of liability.
solution: Sell trusteeship of a well covenant, not sensors. (1) A paste-in Covenant Kit for county attorneys: development-agreement rider, trust instrument, enrollment rules, and a published trigger protocol. (2) Trigger design: 8-12 upgradient control wells outside the cone of influence, a 12-month pre-construction regression of each enrolled household well on the control wells, and the developer's metered pumping records shared with the panel. A trigger fires only on sustained deviation beyond the control-adjusted trend (for example >5 ft and >2 standard errors for 30 days), so the developer pays for excess drawdown and not for drought. (3) Remedy is in kind, not cash indemnity: emergency water hauling in 24-48 hours, then pump lowering or well deepening by a pre-qualified local driller at a fixed rate card. The developer is the obligor and a corporate trustee (a regional bank trust department) holds the escrow. We are administrator and data steward and never hold the money. That structure is closer to a remediation trust or warranty than to an insurance policy, and a counsel opinion is the gate. (4) Governance: a 3-person technical panel with one member appointed by the county (ideally from state extension or the geological survey), one by the developer and one by a residents' council. (5) Hardware and labs are bought from KETOS, Eno Scientific, Kunak-type vendors. Noise, PM2.5 and voltage are paid add-ons later.
why_now: Permit politics moved to governors in 2026 (NY Executive Order 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ permit halt on Sept 21), and counties are writing the rules now. Franklin County's draft already contains developer-paid monitoring wells, a licensed-hydrogeologist assessment and an escrow for 24-hour potable water to impacted neighbors. Shenandoah County officials back applicant-funded third-party testing, and St. Louis's permit requires a developer-funded hydraulic study. Ordinances get copied county to county, so a ready, legally vetted kit written this quarter can become the template. The Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) shows what a baseline-less well dispute costs.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer through the county-mandated covenant. Illustrative program of 500 enrolled households: $1,000 per household setup (mostly hardware pass-through, about 25% margin) = $500k; $480 per household per year for telemetry, QA, lab checks and reporting = $240k per year at about 55% gross margin; administrator fee of 1% per year on a $1.5M remediation reserve (about $2,500 per household) = $15k; $500 per adjudicated claim. Extensions add per-household noise, air and voltage modules. Later: license the trigger protocol and dataset to state agencies and insurers. Assumptions to test: expected remedy claim rate of 5-10% of wells over 10 years, and $8-15k per remedy.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the county attorney, not the developer. Because the county imposes the covenant, the developer's objection to volunteering a payout (an implied admission) disappears, and the county gets an instrument it cannot write itself. The economics are also better for developers than the alternative: NorthPoint offered $10k to each of 4,500 households ($45M) and was accused of bribery, while an in-kind covenant reserve for the households that could plausibly lose water is a small fraction of that and is credible because a neutral panel decides. Attribution is fixed in the design (control wells and pumping records), not argued afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: get Franklin County IN's draft v3.0 and the Shenandoah County notes, call the county attorneys and planning directors, and offer to draft the covenant and trust instrument free in exchange for being named in the draft. Days 3-14: retain a land-use or insurance-regulatory lawyer for a written view on insurance characterization (remediation trust, developer as obligor, in-kind remedy); recruit a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and two regional bank trust departments as prospective corporate trustee. Days 10-30: run the parent's 10-neighbor-well pilot in a county with a pending hearing, but with control wells and the regression trigger back-tested on 12 months of public USGS or state well data, and bring the term sheet plus live dashboard to the hearing. Kill gate at 90 days: one developer or county puts a funded escrow in writing and counsel signs off; otherwise stop.

title: Special-Ed Parent Tracker Feeding Host-School Programs
one_liner: A $20-a-month IEP chief of staff for Texas parents whose service-minute logs identify the families and districts where a clinician-led, voucher-funded host-school program is the real solution.
customer: Texas parents of children with IEPs, reached through special-ed parent groups and pediatric practices, some holding Texas Education Freedom Account (TEFA) funds of about $10K, up to about $30K for IEP students at accredited private schools. Partner: small accredited private schools with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists.
problem: The parent tracker has a low-ARPU, high-CAC consumer business at $20 per month. The host-school program has a high-value payer but no cheap way to find qualified families or to decide where to site a cohort. Parents with documented missed services and a stalled district are stuck, and the money that could fix it is locked behind accreditation and a two-year operating history that they do not have.
solution: Parents upload the IEP and get a legal clock, a service-minute log, records requests and meeting briefs (independent advocates on demand at $75 per 30 minutes). When the log shows sustained missed minutes, the parent sees a clearly labeled 'Plan B' in the app: apply their TEFA funds at a clinician-led program running inside a partner accredited school, where the school is school of record and the operating company supplies the clinical director, staff, curriculum, IEP-style compliance, testing and ESA billing. Firewall: advocate income is flat-fee and never tied to placement, and parents get the compensatory-services claim documented before they leave. First sellable products: the Texas parent subscription plus a January 2027 pilot cohort of 8-10 students at one host school.
why_now: TEFA's first year is underway (2026-27) with $1B in funding and 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students and are closing campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in Oct 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are actively looking for alternatives and an organized paper trail.
revenue_model: Parent subscriptions at $20 per month, advocate sessions at $75 with a revenue split to a vetted co-op, and per-member fees from parent centers and pediatric groups. Host-program management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student (about $6-7.5K per $30K student, $60-75K per 10-student program per year), a 15-20% host-school share, plus a $3-5K design fee per host.
non_obvious_insight: A parent's service-minute log is both a legal claim and a qualified lead: it documents exactly who is failing, in which district, for which disability. Aggregated (with consent), the logs form a district-level heat map that tells the operating company where to place the next host program, because demand is proven in the data. One placed student is worth about 25 years of a $20 subscription in a single year, which pays for the tracker's whole acquisition cost, while the tracker's advocate-first brand makes the placement offer credible rather than salesy.
first_30_days: Publish a free Texas IEP clock calculator and letter templates. With admins of 10 state-level special-ed groups, concierge 30 families and measure violations found. List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin and send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from the 30 concierge families and TEFA parent groups.
lineage: hybrid of I0289 + I1032 (IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents + AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools). Why stronger: The tracker's CAC is subsidized by a payer worth an order of magnitude more per family, and the host program gets pre-qualified, motivated, documented leads instead of buying ads. Shared data tells the business where to open programs. Together it is a full lifecycle (enforce, then exit if enforcement fails) that a competitor with only one half cannot offer.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Fusion Academy (Nord Anglia), Brightmont Academy, Prenda (microschool platform), KaiPod Learning. White space: Research caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any searches ran, so this verdict rests on about 30 direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. Google-style discovery of funded startups was not possible, and the negative finding below is unproven. Crunchbase (403), the Comptroller TEFA program pages (404), TEPSAC (503) and several news sites failed.

What the fetches found: no direct competitor was located that runs clinician-led disability programs inside host accredited private schools as the school-of-record structure and bills against TEFA. Adjacent players cover each piece separately.
- Learning-differences schools that build their own campuses: Fusion, Brightmont, Rawson Saunders, Fairhill.
- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.
- Outside operators embedded in private schools: Catapult.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:
1. **Legality and accreditor acceptance.** Statute text says a private school must be accredited by a TEPSAC-recognized organization and have continuously operated a campus for at least two school years. It does not address programs within a school or microschools. If the Comptroller, TEA or the accreditor treats a hosted program as a separate campus, or as renting accreditation, the model fails. A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.
2. **Incumbents and hosts.** Existing specialist schools already have eligibility and expertise and may simply expand. Host schools take on IEP compliance liability and reputational risk.
3. **Unit economics.** A 10-student cohort at 20-25% yields $60-75k a year, before clinician cost. Whether that covers a BCBA or dyslexia therapist plus a clinical director was not tested.

title: AP-Inbox Implant Reconciler for Spine ASCs
one_liner: Forward your implant vendor invoices to one email address. We match each to the surgery, the payer's carve-out clause and the 835, and reopen the claim the day the invoice lands, so implant cost stops going unpaid.
customer: Independent, surgeon-owned spine and pain-management (spinal cord stimulator) ASCs doing about 100-600 implant cases a year. They have a one-to-three-person in-house billing office, or an outsourced biller paid a percentage of collections, and no supply-chain analyst. The buyer is the administrator plus the surgeon-owner who signs off on distributions. Launch in one state through its ASC association so outreach is dense.
problem: The leak is not ignorance of carve-outs (Becker's has covered them since 2014). It is a hand-off race. The claim leaves billing days after surgery. The consignment vendor invoice lands in accounts payable weeks later, if it is ever tied to the case. Sticker-sheet lot numbers, invoice lines and payer attachment rules share no common ID. So the claim goes out at charges, posts as 'paid', and no system emits the event 'invoice arrived for a case already billed'. Corrected-claim and appeal windows then expire silently. Testable hypothesis for the first audits: a meaningful share of implant cases have a claim date earlier than the invoice date. Each miss is worth roughly $5k-30k, and Medicare ASC cases are excluded because they are not carved out.
solution: (1) Zero-integration intake. Vendor invoices are auto-forwarded from the AP inbox, QuickBooks or Bill.com. An LLM extracts line items (manufacturer, catalog, lot, UDI-DI, unit price). The case schedule or implant log comes as a CSV or photos of sticker sheets, and the ERAs are pulled from the clearinghouse. No EHR or practice-management integration. (2) Rule engine with a payer-clause library. Contract PDFs are LLM-extracted and human-verified once, then reused across every ASC with the same payer. For workers' comp and no-fault, the engine uses public state fee schedules, several of which pay implants at invoice cost plus a capped markup (verify per state). This removes the 'read every contract' scaling limit. (3) The trigger. When an invoice matches a case already billed at $0 or bundled, it auto-builds the payer-specific attachment packet and corrected claim or appeal, ranked by days left to timely filing. Coders file for the first year, then automation. (4) A weekly one-page 'implant cash gap' for the administrator: unmatched invoices, invoice lag by vendor, payers paying $0.
why_now: ASC volume is shifting toward device-heavy musculoskeletal cases. CMS's CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) is reported to add more of them; verify the exact list. Becker's ran 'ASCs' implant cost problem' in March 2026 and 'payer terms ASCs can't miss' in July 2026. Payer AI payment-integrity tools now auto-zero claims that lack attachments. LLM invoice extraction, which used to need OCR templates per vendor, is now cents per invoice.
revenue_model: Lookback: 25% of cash actually collected on recovered carve-outs, over a 12-18 month lookback bounded by timely filing, with no fee if nothing is recovered. Then convert to $1.5-2.5k/month per ASC (or about $12 per implant case) for the invoice trigger and weekly digest. Hypothesis to prove in the audits: a 300-implant-case ASC with a 10% leak at about $8k a case is $240k a year, so about $60k of first-year contingency and $18-30k a year of recurring revenue. Fifty ASCs would be roughly $1M+ of ARR plus about $3M of one-time contingency.
non_obvious_insight: The missing thing is an event, not data. Every RCM tool is triggered from the billing side, and nothing in the stack fires when an invoice arrives in AP after the claim is gone. Accounts payable is also the cheapest integration surface in healthcare, since forwarding email needs no IT project, so time-to-first-dollar is days. The wedge also counter-positions against billers. A percentage-of-collections biller cannot sell 'your billing is incomplete' without indicting itself, and the AP-side product never asks to replace them.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM or call 40 spine/SCS ASC administrators and surgeon-owners in one state via its ASC association and LinkedIn, offering a free 12-month lookback at 25% of cash collected only. Sign 3 design partners with a BAA. Week 2: pull 12 months of 835s, case and implant logs, and the AP invoice folder. Extract invoices with an LLM and spot-check to at least 95% line accuracy. Hand-read each site's top 3 commercial carve-out clauses. Week 3: match and measure three things. These are the share of implant cases where the claim predates the invoice, the implant lines paid $0 or bundled where the clause says carve-out, and the dollars still inside timely filing. Week 4: file the first 15-25 corrected claims and appeals, write a one-page anonymized leak report, and start outbound to 40 more ASCs. Gate: continue only if at least 2 of 3 sites show identifiable, collectible leakage of at least 3% of implant spend. Otherwise narrow to newly opened or converted ASCs, or kill.

ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists. | How this version avoids them: Aspirion (ContractIQ), FinThrive Contract Manager, Sift RevProtect, Waystar and MDaudit all start from claims and contract models sold to hospital revenue-cycle teams. None ingest vendor AP invoices or fire on invoice arrival, and they are retrospective variance tools, not per-case attachment and corrected-claim builders. This product is sold to the ASC owner and administrator as a supply-chain-to-cash control, which those enterprise sellers do not reach. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways sit in the practice-management and billing workflow that this product deliberately stays outside, so it works with any biller or PM system. Defensibility comes from the cross-ASC payer-clause library and invoice-lag dataset, which is a cornered resource, and from the switching cost of becoming the ASC's implant ledger. If Aspirion bolts on contract-level carve-outs, it still needs the AP-side intake and the ASC-owner sale.

title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.

The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. title: Notarized Mitigation Records: The Evidence Standard for Wildfire Credits
one_liner: A score-agnostic verification layer where contractors capture signed photos that are cross-checked against imagery and issued as portable machine-readable Verified Mitigation Records, which carriers and certifiers accept.
customer: First, Front Range defensible-space crews, roofers, ember-vent installers and drone inspectors, who pay per job. Then wildfire certification programs (Wildfire Partners, IBHS-style programs) that pay per avoided inspection. Then carriers' appeal desks and underwriters, who read the record through a free API and later pay for ingestion. HOAs and fire-safe councils are the bulk channel.
problem: Homeowners spend $5k-$30k hardening a house and cannot prove it in a way an insurer will accept. Photos and photo-log templates are easy to fake, and AI image generation makes unverified photos worth less each year. HB25-1182 obliges insurers to credit documented mitigation but sets no evidence standard, and on-site inspection capacity is the bottleneck. Contractors cannot promise an insurance credit, so hardening jobs stay unsold.
solution: A web app (PWA first) for contractors and homeowners with guided capture: a checklist of shots for Zone 0/1/2, vents, roof and gutters, taken with signed capture (C2PA-style content credentials, device attestation, GPS, time and heading). The system cross-checks each claim against archived and new imagery and lidar, for example that vegetation was cleared between two dated images or that a roof is Class A. It issues a Verified Mitigation Record as an open-schema JSON file plus a PDF, versioned and portable across carriers. The schema is published under an open licence and co-developed with a fire-safe council. Carrier and certifier readers are free, and acceptance outcomes feed a per-carrier acceptance dataset. The capture layer would use an existing signed-capture SDK, not a new one.
why_now: Generative image tools have made unverified photo evidence untrustworthy. Signed-capture standards and SDKs are now commodity. HB25-1182 turned documented mitigation into a legal object with no format. High-resolution archives and public lidar are cheap enough to act as the independent witness. This is also the inversion of the parent idea: instead of proving a model wrong about the house, prove the house right and let any score-maker read it.
revenue_model: $49-$89 per notarized job, paid by the contractor and passed through in the quote. $40-$120 per avoided on-site reinspection from certification programs. $15-$60 per accepted record from carriers via subscription or API. Agents from a rebuttal desk buy per file. At 300 contractors doing 40 records a year at $65, that is about $0.8M, and the carrier and certifier layers scale it much further.
non_obvious_insight: The reason insurers can decline third-party imagery is that they cannot trust or parse it, not that they are hostile. Give them evidence with provenance, in a schema they can auto-ingest, and the cost of handling an appeal falls. The parent's moat, the concession database, then extends into a network: contractors, homeowners and carriers all gain from a shared format, as with ACORD forms or the Uniform Appraisal Dataset. Because the layer describes the house and not the score, it holds up when Zesty, Cotality or Verisk change their models, and it is neutral in a way a scorer can never be.
first_30_days: Sign 5 Boulder and Jefferson County defensible-space and roofing contractors on a free pilot. Ship the guided-capture PWA with the imagery cross-check. Notarize 60 real jobs. Ask 3 agencies to submit those records in real credit requests and log carrier responses. Propose a 10-file remote pre-verification pilot to Wildfire Partners. Publish schema v0.1 on GitHub.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.

title: Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families
one_liner: A flat-fee, advocate-supervised 'estate file' service that gets a dead parent's or grandfather's land, shares and dormant accounts legally transferred, sold to the adult children who pay from Nairobi, Dallas or Dubai.
customer: Salaried urban and diaspora Kenyans aged 30-55 whose rural parents or grandparents died (or are old) with land still registered in a dead person's name. They pay from abroad or from the city. A secondary B2B payer is any SACCO, coop or bank that needs cleared successions before it releases deposits or lends against land.
problem: Most rural family land is still titled to a dead grandfather or father because nobody completed succession. The process needs a chief's letter, a death certificate, consents from every heir, gazettement, a wait before confirmation of grant, and then transmission at the land registry, which is often 1-3 years and many trips. Until it is done the land cannot be leased, mortgaged, subdivided or cleanly sold, siblings fight, and the deceased's SACCO deposits, coop shares, insurance and pension sit unclaimed. The real blocker is coordinating 8 to 20 relatives to sign, not the court.
solution: Wedge product is a 'Family Estate Map' for roughly KES 15-25k (pricing to be tested). The child sends photos of the title, IDs, death certificate and old share certificates over WhatsApp. An LLM pipeline extracts names and parcel numbers, handles the multiple-name and spelling-variant problem in Kenyan naming, builds the family tree and likely heirs, and lists the consents needed. It runs official land searches and asset-discovery letters to SACCOs, coops, insurers and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, then outputs a court-ready bundle of forms and affidavits. A home-county field agent collects the chief's letter and relatives' signatures or thumbprints, with video proof of consent. Partner advocates then file and shepherd the case at their own scale fees. Later upsells are surveyor subdivision and lease or loan readiness.
why_now: The generation that took up land in the 1960s-80s through settlement schemes and land-buying companies is dying now, so the succession backlog is peaking. Diaspora remittances are near record levels (roughly US$5bn a year), and families increasingly ask 'sort out the land' rather than 'build a house'. Digitised land records (Ardhisasa) and court e-filing reduce physical running, though their current coverage needs checking. LLMs can now read messy scanned title and ID documents and draft forms in English while chatting with clients in Swahili. I could not run live searches, so verify current UFAA agent rules, court e-filing scope for successions, and fee schedules before building.
revenue_model: Flat fee per estate file, paid by M-Pesa or card from abroad. Advocate fees are billed by the advocates themselves, so the company sells software and case management and does not split fees with non-lawyers. Asset discovery is a flat add-on fee, not a percentage cut of UFAA payouts, because UFAA discourages middlemen taking a share. B2B revenue is per cleaned member estate from SACCOs and coops. Later there is referral income from surveyors and land-backed lenders once titles are clean.
non_obvious_insight: Rural Kenya's biggest pool of unused collateral is land trapped in the name of the dead. The bottleneck is family coordination and evidence gathering, so the product is a coordination workflow sold to the sibling who has money and guilt, not a land registry or a lawyer marketplace. VCs looking at land-tech miss that the payer is the diaspora child, not the farmer.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Murang'a or Kakamega) and recruit two advocates who already do succession work. Build intake on WhatsApp Business, Airtable and an LLM extraction script. Sell 10 files at a pilot discount through your own family network, church and alumni groups, and diaspora WhatsApp and Facebook groups such as Kenyans in Texas or the UK. Publish a free 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' checker as lead-gen. Track days from intake to gazettement as the core metric.
