title: Outsourced Large-Load Intake Desk for Co-op Pools
one_liner: A stage-gated, applicant-paid intake administrator and cross-utility duplicate registry for G&T co-op pools outside ERCOT, so 5-person planning staffs only ever see evidence-backed projects.
customer: Wedge: one mid-size G&T (or state co-op association planning group) outside ERCOT, in SPP, MISO or the Mountain West, that fields 8+ large-load inquiries a year and has 1-2 planners eating the load (Central Electric Power Cooperative's lead spends about 40% of his time on data centers). The G&T adopts the desk by board resolution, and the applicant pays through a filed fee schedule, following Great River Energy's bill-the-petitioner model. Second ring: the G&T's 20-40 distribution co-ops, then neighboring G&Ts.
problem: The judges' central worry was right. Collateral, study fees and site-control rules are making applicants self-prove, so a 12-point memo shop sells checks the applicant will soon hand over anyway. Equipment slots and financing letters are also confidential, and real developers often call the utility before they order equipment. Meanwhile the co-op still has no staff to run intake and no way to see that the same 300 MW is being shopped to five utilities. Regulators are absorbing LLC transparency at the state level (Texas audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 order for projects over 25 MW), which weakens any pure-LLC-lookup product.
solution: Run intake as an operated service, not a memo. (1) Evidence ladder tied to money release. Gate 0 (intake fee paid): public-record checks only, which is what any real developer already has: LLC principals across states, recorded deed or option, air-permit pre-application and generator count vs. claimed MW, water and stormwater filings, and claimed energization date vs. published transformer and switchgear lead times. Gate 1 (study deposit released): named references (OEM, EPC, tenant, lender officer) verified by phone, with a signed attestation and a misrepresentation clause that forfeits the deposit. Gate 2 (ESA signature): redacted OEM order acknowledgment and financing confirmation. Early gates test only what an early-stage real project has; unobservable items are pushed to the gate where money is at risk. (2) Consent clause: the application form has the applicant consent to share LLC, principals, parcel APN, POI substation, MW ask and status with a pooled registry, which solves the confidentiality problem. The registry matches on parcel, substation POI and principal, not company name, because shells rename themselves but land parcels and substations do not. It returns hits like 'this parcel and principal appear in 3 other territories.' (3) Outputs are structured records that drop into GridUnity or PowerClerk as the pre-queue front door.
why_now: Tariffs and collateral rules are landing (Texas SB 6 final rule due by 12/31/2026, AEP Ohio-style deposits), and Exelon's pipeline fell about 40% and AEP Ohio's more than half once fees and collateral arrived. Every co-op now has to decide what its intake rules are, and most have no staff to run them. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so boards are burned. Cleanview-class permit data has made the public-record layer cheap to assemble and license. Nobody yet runs a duplicate registry outside ERCOT, where SB 6 mandates duplicate disclosure only inside the state.
revenue_model: $20-30K one-time G&T setup (intake policy, fee schedule, ESA rider, board presentation). Applicant-paid intake fees scaled by MW, $10K under 100 MW up to $40K over 500 MW, plus a $15-30K Gate 1 verification fee. The utility keeps a 15% admin share and the desk keeps 85%. A $36K/yr G&T floor retainer covers slow quarters. Registry seats at $12K/yr for utilities outside the pool later. Bottom-up: 3 G&Ts x about 25 paid intakes x about $20K is $1.5M in year 1 at about 80% gross margin, with the registry as the compounding asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fee and the gates are themselves the phantom filter. Shell LLCs will not pay $15K to be verified, and real developers spending $2B+ will not blink. So the desk's real product is converting scarce planner hours into a queue that carries only evidence-backed projects, and detection is a side effect. The staged ladder fixes the 'real developers come before they order equipment' flaw by demanding equipment proof only at the gate where the utility's money is at risk. And the registry keys on parcels and POI substations, physical objects a phantom cannot rename, which is why it holds up even as LLC-disclosure rules improve.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get the last 10-15 inquiries from two co-op contacts via a state association or G&T planning group. Back-test them to show how the ones that died would have scored at Gate 0 and Gate 1. Stand up scrapers for air-permit databases in 4-6 states and deed and Secretary of State records in 2-3 territories, and license Cleanview-style permit data instead of rebuilding it. Days 10-20: write the 2-page intake policy, fee schedule and misrepresentation-clause template. Present the back-test and template to the G&T planning head and ask for a 90-day pilot that starts fees on the next new inquiry, free for existing ones. Days 20-30: interview 5 developers with real projects to test that they would pay $10-15K at intake. Close 1 G&T pilot and process the first paid intake. Kill test: if no G&T will let applicants be billed, or 0 of 5 real developers accept the fee, the applicant-pays thesis is dead.

Enverus, LandGate, GridCARE and ZEG sit on the developer side or in forecasting, and this desk works for the utility and is adverse to the applicant. Cleanview is a public tracker and cannot hold confidential cross-utility inquiry data, so it becomes a licensed input rather than a competitor. NRECA offers free checklists but cannot run a fee-collecting, data-holding, liability-bearing intake operation, so its state associations are the resale channel. Hourly consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) could copy the checks but not the pooled registry economics. Memos were the entry product; the pooled registry across co-ops is the business, and it gets better with every co-op added.

title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure.

title: Holdout Ledger: Landowner-Side Assembly Intelligence
one_liner: The landowner's half of the courthouse tape. It shows farm families and heirs in an assembly corridor who is buying around them, how close the buyer is to finishing, and how much leverage the last holdouts have, paid on closing.
customer: Owners of 100-2,000 acres in counties where recorded options and easements cluster, reached through ag and land-use attorneys, county farm bureaus, rural lenders and direct mail. Wedge: heirs, tenants-in-common and absentee owners who get anonymous offers under NDA. The payer is the landowner, on a contingent fee, plus subscribing law firms.
problem: Each landowner is approached alone by a landman working for an anonymous LLC. NDAs stop neighbors comparing notes. The developer sees the whole assembly and the owner sees one offer. Owners sign early and cheap, or hold out blindly, and cannot tell whether their parcel is a keystone or an afterthought. Landmen work for the buyer, local lawyers rarely have county-wide data, and county officials learn of the project from a leaked story.
solution:
1. 'Neighbor Check': enter a parcel or address and get a map of recorded instruments within about 5 miles, classified from the image. It shows the LLC family behind them, the share of the plausible footprint already recorded, whether the parcel sits on a critical path (contiguity, road access, a line crossing), expiring options, and a plain-English read of what the pattern usually means.
2. Owners in a cluster can opt into a negotiating pool, like the mineral-owner associations in oil and gas leasing. A licensed land broker or attorney partner represents them. We supply the analytics and take a success fee on closing.
3. We sell a group map subscription to ag and land-use law firms and farm-bureau chapters.
why_now: The 2025-26 large-load land rush has put anonymous NDA'd offers in front of thousands of rural owners, and local fights over data center land deals are widely reported. Owners can now see the buyer's footprint because public recorded memoranda can be read at scale with LLM vision. FinCEN's exemption for domestic companies means owners cannot ask who is behind the LLC and get a federal answer, so primary records are the only route. Reported prices such as roughly $100k an acre offered near Hill County, Texas, make the information gap worth real money to owners.
revenue_model: Free lookup as lead generation. $149-$399 for a full parcel report. A contingent success fee of 1.5%-3% of total consideration at closing, collected through a licensed broker affiliate. Example: a 300-acre owner closing a $4M option-plus-lease package yields $60k-$120k. $300-$800 a month per law firm or farm-bureau seat. Ten closed deals in year one is roughly $500k-$1M, at very low marginal cost after the data pull.
non_obvious_insight: The developer's own recorded memoranda reveal how complete the assembly is, and holdout value peaks in the last 20-30% of parcels. That is the moment owners are least informed. Every existing vendor's paying customer is the developer, so none can serve the counterparty without alienating buyers. That is counter-positioning in Helmer's sense. Landowners are numerous, each needs the service once, and assessor rolls are public, so mail reaches them cheaply. The demand is one-shot and high-stakes, which suits a contingent fee better than SaaS. The data burden is also small: a few dozen instruments per cluster, pulled per parcel, with none of the statewide bulk-ingestion risk.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a visible assembly. The parent's method of pulling 24 months of instruments gives the pattern. Mail 400 landowners within the cluster a letter with a QR code: 'Three LLCs using the same law firm recorded options on X acres within 4 miles of your land.' Offer a free Neighbor Check, then a $199 report. Sign a referral and co-marketing agreement with one licensed land broker and one ag attorney. Get 5 owners into a pooled negotiation and 20 paid reports. Before launch, have counsel confirm the broker-licensing and fee-sharing rules in the state (lawyers generally cannot split fees with non-lawyers), and use only public records. We are never a party to any NDA.
lineage: mutation of I0773 ('Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: ATTOM, Regrid, Reonomy, PropertyRadar, Enverus, Paces, Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, GridCARE and Pandell all sell to developers, investors, utilities or the trade. None serves the seller, and none could do so without conflicting with its own customers. Generic land brokerages sell listings but do not read recorded non-deed instruments or unmask LLC families. Landman firms work for the buyer. Nothing in the research offers owners a cluster map or holdout-leverage view. The bulk-access risk is avoided because the work is targeted, parcel by parcel, within a county already showing activity. Weaknesses: a developer or its counsel may push back, some states restrict non-lawyer negotiation help, and reputation matters in small communities.
